en: Paeon has always been configured in one file, which you can keep in a git repository.
Version zero point four adds a second way: the browser.
On a new server, three variables are enough.
A token for your alert senders, a key that protects what the console stores, and console equals local.
There is no rules file to write.
The first time you open the console, it asks for a code.
Paeon printed it in its own log when it started, so only someone who can read that log can use it.
Then you choose the admin password.
The incidents page then lists what is left to do.
Connect a source, send a first alert, choose where Paeon tells you.
Each step has its button, and the list goes away once it is done.
For Prometheus, give its server, a read-only token, and the metrics an investigation may query.
Save and test.
It answers, and it is connected at once, with no restart.
A channel works the same way: ntfy, Telegram, e-mail, and eight more.
Choose what it carries, the digest, the analysis, and a test message goes out.
Approvals are never on that list: the executor sends them, from its own file.
A secret typed here is encrypted before it is stored, and never shown again.
Point a channel somewhere else, and its secrets must be typed again.
The rules file is never written. Its entries are locked, and they win on a name both define.
Behind your proxy, roles come from its groups.
A viewer reads. An operator rates triage and stops automation. An admin changes sources and channels.
Start in the browser.
Move to git when you want. The file always wins.
